title: The Rebirth of the Circus

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For a child in provincial New Zealand in the 1970s, a visit from the circus was the impossible come to life, an unforgettable performance by clowns, acrobats and trained animals all under a magical tent, even if the adults judged the skills on display as strictly second rate. Times have changed, however, and these days the travelling circus is a corporate machine. Along the way the circus has been sanitised and professionalised, its performances today more likely to be seen in a vast, concrete stadium than the small, romantic tents so often associated with the circus in the past. Without doubt, the advent of a diploma in circus arts is part of this trend.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Nonetheless, at CircoArts something of the old disorder of the circus remains. 'Everyone on the course is in some sense a misfit,' says Sarah Mason, a student on the CircoArts diploma. 'We all have this thing that draws us, a feeling that we want something different from life.' Mason was attracted to the programme because of its emphasis on creativity and self-expression as opposed to the more vocational and technical training offered elsewhere. Mason's classmate, Andrew Cook, has always been a nomad. His parents were a teacher and a nurse, and the family frequently moved between different isolated communities in the Australian outback. In his early 20s, having abandoned studies in computer science, he picked up his first set of juggling sticks. 'I did it for six straight hours, he says, 'and was addicted.'

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the teachers on the course is Stanislav Shchukin, who spent 35 years with the Moscow Circus during its golden years. He is 70 now, but still a tough figure with the light step of the gymnast he was for three and a half decades. In Russia, circus has always been regarded as special rather than fringe, and this meant a number of perks: Shchukin's application to live in central Moscow was rubber-stamped. 'And as a circus, we always had the very best,' he says, 'the best costumes and the best orchestra. His partner in the ring was an extremely thin man, and Shchukin would always make a big display of counting the man's ribs to get a laugh out of the audience. This is important, he says, because humour is one of the three key elements of the circus. In order to highlight the others, he tells the story of how he fell in love with the circus. He was a young man when he saw a lovely woman standing on the back of an elegant horse and he realised then that the circus needed displays of this kind of beauty in order to succeed. Then soon after, sitting in an audience that hardly dared breathe, he watched a man dancing on the high wire and saw how everyone in the crowd was captivated by the tightrope walker's courage, which according to Shchukin is the third essential characteristic that everyone wants to see at the circus.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Shchukin's understanding of the circus arts is clearly rubbing off on his young students, and when talking to them you constantly hear his ideas played back to you. In that regard he is the master of something more than just skills at CircoArts: he is initiating a group who weren't raised in the same way as previous generations of performers into the culture of the traditional circus. At the same time, there is also a sense that Shchukin is disenchanted with some elements of the modern circus. He believes that in the new-look troupes of circus performers, the artists are treated as cogs, mere technicians. 'Today,' he says, 'the businessmen who run circuses don't want heroic performances.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Their classrooms might look like playrooms, but those enrolled at CircoArts still need to pass their assessments like any other students. As well as acrobatics, juggling and other technical skills associated with circus, they are also instructed in anatomy, diet and circus history. 'The public sometimes see us as peripheral but they don't understand some of the challenges,' says Godfrey Simms, director of the CircoArts programme. 'The students here are fusing creativity with the discipline of an athlete.' It can be a difficult time for them, adds Simms. Most live communally in a couple of basic properties close to campus. Then there are the bumps and bruises that the students pick up in training. Dan Hales, one of the older students, has had his share. At the moment, he is recovering from yet another strain, this one to his neck. 'As soon as you get over one thing, you get the next one,' he says.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: His classmate Neisha Murphy agrees that it's hard work. She says, 'You think you're going to be happy when you master a particular trick, but it's never like that. You only think about what's next.' One of the most difficult things is to build trust with your partner, adds Murphy, who does a double trapeze act with a Belgian called Dada. 'I’ve reached the point now where I can fall and just know that he's got me,' she says. 'But it's taken a whole year.' What's the point of all this hard work and suffering then? It's like the famous English clown Reg Bolton once said: circus is the art of doing the pointless, perfectly.
